AI Companies Have a Distribution Problem Disguised as a Model Problem.

Analysislowob research

By lowob · 15 June 2026 · Updated 16 November 2026 · 7-minute read · Distribution

A company can build an impressive AI product, show a great demo, and still struggle to find paying customers. Often the problem is not that the model needs another improvement. It is that the company has not worked out who needs the product, why they should trust it, or how they will discover it. The market evidence points the same way: enterprise AI spend reached about $177 billion in 2026 by Menlo Ventures' estimate, yet buyers increasingly say the models perform well enough, and they now judge AI products on security, cost, integration and proof.

Model quality matters. But better model performance does not automatically create a distribution system. This piece sets out the evidence that the constraint has moved, and a way to tell which problem a company actually has before deciding what to build next. Our explainer on what a go-to-market strategy is covers the wider plan this sits inside.

A better model isn't a go-to-market plan

Picture a small AI company that can summarise and search internal contracts. Its team spends weeks improving response quality. Meanwhile, the potential buyers are asking different questions. Can we connect it to the documents we already use? Who can see sensitive information? How would we check an incorrect answer? Who owns the rollout?

The demonstration proves a capability. It does not yet make the product easy to adopt. This is a hypothetical example, but it captures the gap between building something useful and persuading an organisation to depend on it.

The buyer evidence supports the distinction. Andreessen Horowitz's 2025 survey of 100 CIOs across 15 industries found that "procurement now mirrors traditional software buying", with more rigorous evaluations and more price sensitivity. Security and cost had gained weight relative to accuracy and reliability. One leader put it plainly: "for most tasks, all the models perform well enough now."

Gartner's June 2025 forecast that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027 names escalating costs and unclear business value as the causes. Neither is a model problem. Both are problems of fit, proof and adoption.

A company can still need better technology. The point is to distinguish product problems from distribution and adoption problems before deciding what to build next.

Name the buyer and the job they need done

"Businesses that want to use AI" is too broad to guide marketing. "Legal operations teams that spend hours finding clauses across supplier contracts" is more specific. It points to a job, a person responsible for it, a current alternative and a meaningful outcome.

Start with three questions. Who has the problem often enough to pay? What do they do today instead? What would convince them to change? Interview buyers rather than answering from the product team's imagination. Our guide to writing an ICP sales will use sets out the fields worth recording.

The money is there for companies that answer those questions well. Menlo Ventures' 2026 survey of nearly 400 US enterprise decision makers estimated deployment spend at $176.8 billion through September 2026, up 5.4 times on the prior year. New budgets funded 55% of the incremental spend, and AI-native vendors captured 77% of application-layer spend. Adoption grew more slowly, from 55% to 65% of enterprises, which means spend is concentrating in buyers who have already found a job worth paying for.

Not every AI product needs to own an entire workflow. Some successful products are focused components inside systems customers already use. In either case, the integration and the end result matter more to adoption than the isolated model demo.

Show what the product does, and where it can fail

Trust grows when people can inspect the work. A short demonstration with a real workflow, realistic inputs and clearly identified limitations is more persuasive than a claim that the tool is "revolutionary". In higher-stakes uses, explain what happens when the system is uncertain and how people can review its output.

Buyers are primed to discount broad claims. Gartner estimated in 2025 that only about 130 of the thousands of vendors marketing agentic AI were offering real agentic capability, the practice our explainer on agent washing describes. Gartner's survey of 645 B2B buyers, published in May 2026, found 45% had used generative AI during a purchase, 51% believed they were more likely to get misleading information from it, and 69% preferred to check AI-generated insights with a sales rep. A vendor that makes its proof easy to check is answering the question buyers are already asking.

For the contract product, useful proof might include sample tasks, permission controls, a documented evaluation process and feedback from a pilot customer, with the customer's permission. Avoid claiming a universal accuracy rate based on a small internal test. Our explainer on AI evals covers how to build a test a buyer can read.

The demonstration proves a capability. It does not yet make the product easy to adopt.

The team should record objections from sales calls and use them to improve the product, the explanation and the onboarding process.

Build channels that reach the people doing the work

Generic AI announcements compete with thousands of similar launches. An industry practitioner demonstrating a workflow, an integration into software buyers already use, or a useful comparison published where teams research solutions may do more to reach a qualified buyer.

The data on how AI products are adopted backs this. Menlo's 2025 survey of 495 US enterprise AI decision makers found 27% of AI application spend came through product-led growth, against 7% in traditional software. Adoption often started with individual users who proved value in daily work before any central contract. Menlo reported that Cursor reached $200 million in revenue before hiring an enterprise sales rep. That is one company, reported by an investor, but the pattern across the survey is consistent: in AI, the person doing the work often finds the product first.

Prioritise a few channels you can test: direct conversations with target accounts, credible practitioner partnerships, integrations and instructional content. Cloud marketplaces can shorten procurement once a buyer is interested, as our piece on marketplace listings for B2B explains. Add paid acquisition where the economics make sense and the claims are supportable. Keep the resulting contacts and learning in systems the company controls.

Choose a distribution approach that remains useful even if the underlying models improve or suppliers change. Menlo's 2026 data shows how fast the supply side moves: Google's share of enterprise model API spend fell from 21% to 9% in a year while Anthropic's rose from 40% to 55%. A channel built on the buyer and the workflow survives those swings. A pitch built on whichever model leads this quarter does not.

Measure adoption, not demo applause

Track the path from a relevant conversation to a trial, a completed job, repeat use and, when applicable, paid retention. If the product's value is saving time, measure the quality of the result alongside the time saved. A faster answer that creates rework is not a win.

Conversion is achievable. Menlo's 2025 survey found 47% of AI deals reached production, against 25% for traditional SaaS. The companies that convert are those whose pilots end in a completed job a buyer can point to.

When prospects consistently fail at setup, improve onboarding. When nobody can explain the return, improve proof. When the right people never see the product, improve distribution. Those are different problems, and they deserve different responses.

What you seeWhat kind of problem it isThe response
Strong demo reactions, few trialsReach or targetingNarrow the buyer; test practitioner and integration channels
Trials start, setup stallsAdoptionFix onboarding, connectors and permissions before features
Trials complete, no purchaseProof or valuePublish the eval; tie the result to the buyer's own cost
Purchases, low repeat useProduct or fitRevisit the job; this is where model or workflow work pays
Repeat use, slow expansionDistribution inside the accountName the next team and the owner who will carry it

Only one row in that table is primarily a model problem. Most AI companies that believe they need a better model are sitting in one of the other four.

lowob takeaways

  • Separate capability from adoption. A better model alone will not fix a missing buyer or channel.
  • Sell a specific job. State who needs the product, what they do today and what improves.
  • Make proof easy to inspect. Real workflow examples and honest limitations build more trust than broad claims, and buyers now check.
  • Measure repeat use. Trials and demos matter only if the product becomes useful work.

Common questions

Why do AI startups struggle to get customers even with a good product?

Usually because the company has not named a specific buyer and job, made its proof easy to check, or built a channel that reaches the people doing the work. Buyers increasingly say models perform well enough for most tasks, so they judge on fit, security, cost and evidence.

How do you know if an AI company has a product problem or a distribution problem?

Look at where prospects stop. Few trials point to reach; stalled setup points to onboarding; completed trials without purchase point to proof; purchases without repeat use point to product fit. Only the last is mainly a model problem.

Why are so many enterprise AI projects cancelled?

Gartner expects more than 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027, citing escalating costs and unclear business value. Projects without a defined job, owner and success measure are the most exposed.

What distribution channels work best for AI products?

Channels that reach practitioners: direct conversations with target accounts, integrations into tools buyers already use, practitioner partnerships and instructional content. Product-led adoption carried 27% of AI application spend in Menlo's 2025 survey, against 7% for traditional software.

Sources and notes

  • Menlo Ventures, 2026: The State of Enterprise AI, 3 November 2026. Investor research; nearly 400 US enterprise decision makers surveyed by Morning Consult, 8 to 26 September 2026. Menlo invests in AI companies.
  • Menlo Ventures, 2025: The State of Generative AI in the Enterprise, 9 December 2025. Investor research; 495 US enterprise AI decision makers, November 2025. Private-company revenue figures are Menlo's estimates.
  • Andreessen Horowitz, How 100 Enterprise CIOs Are Building and Buying Gen AI in 2025, 10 June 2025. Investor research; 100 CIOs plus interviews, data as of May 2025.
  • Reuters via The Star, Over 40% of agentic AI projects will be scrapped by 2027, Gartner says, 25 June 2025. News report of a Gartner prediction; the 130-vendor figure is Gartner's estimate.
  • Gartner, Survey Finds 69% of B2B Buyers Turn to Sales Reps to Validate AI-Generated Insights, 20 May 2026. Survey of 645 B2B buyers, August to September 2025; all categories, not only AI purchases.
  • The contract example is hypothetical, and the diagnostic table is lowob's framework. No client outcomes are claimed.

Pull the last twenty prospects who saw a demo and mark where each one stopped: no trial, stalled setup, no purchase or low repeat use. Fix the row with the most names before you schedule the next model improvement.
